anchor.quote: people use a small number of predictive cues to place parties, though more politically sophisticated voters draw from a broader set of policies, values, and constituencies.

claims.note:
Fix: Footnote omits the authors; add "Seonghui Lee, Lie Philip Santoso, and Randolph Stevenson" and the subtitle.
Finding: The cited work exists and says precisely this. *Heuristic Inference and the Left-Right: An Experimental Analysis of How Voters Form Their Left-Right Images of Parties*, by Seonghui Lee, Lie Philip Santoso, and Randolph Stevenson, Cambridge Elements in Experimental Political Science, 2026 (online June 26, 2026). Conjoint experiments in Canada, Denmark, Germany, UK; voters infer party left-right positions from policy, value, partisan-cooperation, and social-group cues; less sophisticated voters lean on partisan signals, more sophisticated voters "draw from a broader range of indicators, including party policies, ideological values, and social group support."

anchor.quote: economic and cultural attitudes can be separated both conceptually and empirically.[^4] Second, no universal factor structure settles politics once and for all.

Finding: Both cited works exist and support the sentences as written. Feldman & Huddy argue "political ideology is best explained by at least two dimensions linked to economic and social ideology." anchor.quote: Culture, coercion, and belonging formed a strong contemporary bundle, correlating at roughly .78 to .82. claims.note:
Fix: none required; publishing the composite definitions (even in a footnote or linked appendix) would make the exercise checkable by readers. Phase 3 should note the .78–.90 bundle is the strongest ammunition for a "that's just one cultural dimension in Europe" objection.
Finding: Author's own exploratory analysis; exact values depend on unstated variable choices, but the pattern **reproduces**. I downloaded CHES 2024 and built plausible composites (economy: lrecon/redistribution/deregulation/spendvtax; culture: galtan/womens_rights/lgbtq_rights/samesex_marriage/religious_principles; coercion: civlib_laworder/executive_power; belonging: nationalism/immigrate_policy/multiculturalism/ethnic_minorities; system: anti_elite_salience/people_v_elite). Result: culture–coercion–belonging pairwise r = .84–.90 (draft: .78–.82); economy vs those three r = .47–.56 (draft: .39–.56); system vs economy r = −.13 (single vars: lrecon×anti_elite_salience = −.10, lrecon×people_v_elite = −.20) — "slight negative relationship with market economics" confirmed. Draft's stated ranges are consistent with reasonable alternative composites; my reproduction runs slightly higher on the culture bundle.
claims.text: "Culture, coercion, and belonging formed a strong contemporary bundle, correlating at roughly .78 to .82. Economy was related but more independent, with correlations of roughly .39 to .56. The insurgent or anti-establishment measures cut across the others more sharply, including a slight negative relationship with market economics."

anchor.quote: Trump is a populist natcon: market-leaning, authority-oriented, culturally traditional, strongly communal, and insurgent, with unitary and personalist features.

claims.note:
escalated to Tier 1
Fix: Re-score Economy toward "mixed" (a 3, or 4 with an explicit protectionism tag), or split rhetoric/program/practice as §V itself prescribes — e.g., "market-rhetorical, protectionist-statist in practice." This would *strengthen* the essay: Trump is the best available demonstration of its own rhetoric/program/practice distinction.
Finding: "Market-leaning" is not what the mid-2026 record supports on the draft's own Economy axis. Second-term economic policy is tariff-centered and state-directive: a 10% universal baseline tariff (re-imposed under Section 122 after the Supreme Court's Feb 20, 2026 ruling struck the IEEPA tariffs), Section 232 tariffs of 10–50% on steel, aluminum, copper, autos, pharmaceuticals, lumber, furniture; estimated applied tariff rate rising toward ~11.8%; ~$900 average household tax increase in 2026; plus a 9.9% federal equity stake in Intel and a sovereign-wealth-fund initiative putting "government ownership back on the policy agenda." Tax cuts and deregulation exist on the other side of the ledger, so "mixed/protectionist-statist" is defensible — "market-leaning" as the profile's first coordinate is not, and the draft itself warns that "a nominally market-oriented party can construct protectionist policy" (§V) without applying the warning here. Reputationally consequential characterization of a named person; readers will contest it immediately.
claims.text: "Trump is a populist natcon: market-leaning, authority-oriented, culturally traditional, strongly communal, and insurgent, with unitary and personalist features."

anchor.quote: Orbán is a welfare nationalist: economically mixed, authority-oriented, traditional, strongly communal, and populist in legitimation despite governing through a consolidated institutional apparatus.

claims.note:
escalated to Tier 1
Fix: Date the profile ("Orbán in office, 2010–2026") or recast in past tense; the loss of power is itself a usable data point for the essay's insurgent/institutional discussion.
Finding: Currency failure: Orbán is no longer governing. On April 12, 2026, Péter Magyar's Tisza party defeated Fidesz in a landslide (Tisza ~138–141 of 199 seats, a two-thirds supermajority; Fidesz ~55), ending 16 years of Orbán government; Orbán conceded ("The responsibility and possibility of governing was not given to us") and Magyar formed a government. Since the draft cites a June 10, 2026 Pew report, it was written *after* this — the present-tense "governing" is false as written, and the "consolidated institutional apparatus" is being dismantled by a constitutional supermajority. The ideological characterization itself remains sound (C18). Ironic against the draft's own Rule 4, "Date every profile."
claims.text: "Orbán is a welfare nationalist: economically mixed, authority-oriented, traditional, strongly communal, and populist in legitimation despite governing through a consolidated institutional apparatus."
